concepts: Differentiability of piecewise and modulus functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}-1, & -2\le x<0\\ x^2-1, & 0\le x\le 2\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=|f(x)|+f(|x|)$. Then, in the interval $(-2,2)$, $g$ is:
questions.key_idea: Rewrite $g$ piecewise; a kink can only occur where a branch changes, so compare one-sided slopes at $0$ and $1$.
solution: So $g(x)=x^2$ on $[-2,0)$, $0$ on $[0,1)$, $2x^2-2$ on $[1,2]$; $g$ is continuous everywhere.
At $x=0$: left derivative $2x=0$ and right derivative $0$, so $g$ is differentiable at $0$.
At $x=1$: left derivative $0$, right derivative $4x=4$; not equal, so $g$ is not differentiable at $x=1$ (the only such point in $(-2,2)$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $|x|\ge0$, $f(|x|)=x^2-1$ always, so $g=|f|+x^2-1$ and $|t|+t=2\max(t,0)$ does the rest.
solution: $\max(x^2-1,0)$ has a corner only where $x^2-1$ changes sign with non-zero slope, i.e. at $x=1$ (as $x\ge0$); $x=-1$ is on the smooth branch $x^2$.
At $x=0$: left slope $2x\to0$, right side is $0$, so smooth. Exactly one point of non-differentiability, $x=1$.

useful_results: $|t|+t=2t^+=2\max(t,0)$ and $|t|-t=2\max(-t,0)$: use this to simplify sums like $|h|+h$.
$h(|x|)$ with $h$ given piecewise: replace the argument by $|x|\ge0$ and only use the branch for $\ge0$ arguments.
A piecewise function is differentiable at a join point iff both branches meet in value and in slope; check continuity first, then slopes.
A zero function on an interval (here $g=0$ on $[0,1)$) is smooth there; kinks appear only at the ends of such pieces if slopes differ.

concepts: Composition of functions: one-one and onto
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be defined as $f(x)=2x-1$ and $g:\mathbb R-\{1\}\to\mathbb R$ be defined as $g(x)=\frac{x-\frac12}{x-1}$. Then the composition function $f(g(x))$ is:
questions.key_idea: $f(g(x))=\frac{x}{x-1}=1+\frac1{x-1}$ never takes the value $1$, and is one-one.
solution: So $f(g(x))$ is defined on $\mathbb R-\{1\}$ with values in $\mathbb R$.
$\frac{x}{x-1}=1+\frac{1}{x-1}$ is strictly decreasing on each of $(-\infty,1)$ and $(1,\infty)$, and for $x<1$ it is below $1$ while for $x>1$ it is above $1$; so it is always one-one.
Its range is $\mathbb R-\{1\}$, because $\frac{x}{x-1}=1$ has no solution.
Range $\neq$ codomain $\mathbb R$, so $f(g(x))$ is not onto: it is one-one but not onto.

alternate_solutions.idea: Chase ranges through the two maps: $g$ is one-one and misses one value, so $f\circ g$ misses $f$ of that value.
solution: $g(x)=1+\frac{1/2}{x-1}$ is a Mobius map: one-one on $\mathbb R-\{1\}$ and its range is $\mathbb R-\{1\}$ (the value $1$ is never reached).
$f(x)=2x-1$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R$, so $f\circ g$ is one-one (composition of one-one maps).
Range of $f\circ g=f(\mathbb R-\{1\})=\mathbb R-\{f(1)\}=\mathbb R-\{1\}$.
This is a proper subset of $\mathbb R$, so $f\circ g$ is one-one but not onto.

useful_results: $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ with $ad-bc\ne0$ is one-one on its domain and its range omits exactly $\frac ac$ (the horizontal asymptote).
Composition: one-one $\circ$ one-one is one-one; $\text{range}(f\circ g)=f(\text{range of }g)$, so onto needs the range of $g$ to be mapped onto the whole codomain.
Quick test of a rational function $y=\frac{x}{x-1}$: solve for $x$ in terms of $y$; any $y$ for which it fails (here $y=1$) is missing from the range.

concepts: Differentiability of the maximum of two functions
questions.question: Let $f:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\max\{-|x|,-\sqrt{1-x^2}\}$. If $K$ be the set of all points at which $f$ is not differentiable, then $K$ has exactly:
questions.key_idea: A maximum of two curves has corners where the curves cross, plus any corner of the active branch; here $x=0$ and $x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$.
solution: The two curves meet when $|x|=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, i.e. $2x^2=1$, $x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}$.
From the graph: $-|x|$ has a corner at $x=0$ (slopes $+1$ and $-1$).

At $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ the active branch changes: left slope $-1$ (from $-|x|=-x$), right slope $\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=+1$; by symmetry $x=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ also has slopes $-1$ and $+1$. So these are corners too.
Number of points of non-differentiability $=3$, i.e. $K=\{-\frac1{\sqrt2},0,\frac1{\sqrt2}\}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF only says 'from graph, number of ND points = 3' with a sketch. No error; the algebra locating the crossing points and the slope comparison at each of the three corners was added so the count is justified.
useful_results: $\max(u,v)$ is non-differentiable where $u=v$ with $u'\neq v'$, and wherever the active branch itself has a corner.
$\max(u,v)=\frac{u+v+|u-v|}{2}$ and $\min(u,v)=\frac{u+v-|u-v|}{2}$.
$\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is smooth on $(-1,1)$ (its slope blows up only at $\pm1$), so corners of $f$ come only from $|x|$ and from crossings.

concepts: Recurrence relation for a function on natural numbers
questions.question: Consider a function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, satisfying $f(1)+2f(2)+3f(3)+\dots+xf(x)=x(x+1)f(x)$ for $x\ge2$, with $f(1)=1$. Then $\frac1{f(2022)}+\frac1{f(2028)}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Subtract the relation for $n$ from that for $n+1$ to get $(n+1)f(n+1)=nf(n)$, so $nf(n)$ is constant.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess $f(n)=\frac1{2n}$ from the first values, verify it satisfies the equation for all $x\ge2$, and note the equation determines $f$ uniquely.
solution: RHS $=x(x+1)\cdot\frac1{2x}=\frac{x+1}{2}$. So the guess satisfies the equation for every $x\ge2$.
Uniqueness: the equation gives $f(x)\,[x(x+1)-x]=f(1)+\dots+(x-1)f(x-1)$, so $f(x)$ is fixed by the earlier values; hence $f(n)=\frac1{2n}$ is the only solution.

useful_results: For $S_x=\sum_{k\le x}kf(k)$ relations of the form $S_x=c(x)f(x)$: subtract consecutive instances; $S_x-S_{x-1}=xf(x)$ turns a sum relation into a recurrence.
If $(n+1)f(n+1)=nf(n)$ then $nf(n)$ is constant, so $f(n)=\frac{C}{n}$; fix $C$ from the first available equation.
Always check which indices the relation is valid for (here $x\ge2$), because $f(1)$ may not fit the final formula ($f(1)=1\ne\frac12$).

concepts: Range of a function involving the greatest integer function
questions.question: If the domain of the function $f(x)=\frac{[x]}{1+x^2}$, where $[x]$ is the greatest integer $\le x$, is $[2,6)$, then its range is:
questions.key_idea: On each $[k,k+1)$, $f=\frac{k}{1+x^2}$ is decreasing, giving four half-open intervals whose union has no gaps.
solution: For $x\in[2,3)$: $f(x)=\frac{2}{1+x^2}$, decreasing from $\frac25$ (attained at $x=2$) towards $\frac15$ (not attained); range $\left(\frac15,\frac25\right]$.
Numerically: $(0.2,0.4]$, $(0.176,0.3]$, $(0.154,0.235]$, $(0.135,0.192]$; each overlaps the next, so there are no gaps.
Union: $\left(\frac5{37},\frac25\right]$ - the largest value $\frac25$ at $x=2$ is attained, the smallest $\frac5{37}$ is not.
questions.correction_note: The PDF lists the four branch formulas and a sketch but never computes the range of each branch or the union; the endpoint values, overlap check and union were added. The answer key (C) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the supremum and infimum, then test one of the 'removed' values in options (A) and (D): if it is attained, the gaps are false.
solution: Maximum: at $x=2$, $f=\frac25$ attained. Every branch value is below this since $\frac{k}{1+x^2}\le\frac{k}{1+k^2}\le\frac25$ for $k\ge2$.
Infimum: as $x\to6^-$, $f\to\frac5{37}$ (not attained). So the range lies in $\left(\frac5{37},\frac25\right]$; options (A),(B) are excluded since $\frac5{26}>\frac5{37}$.

Test $\frac9{29}\approx0.3103$ from option (D): it lies in $\left(0.2,0.4\right]$, the branch $\frac{2}{1+x^2}=\frac9{29}$ gives $x^2=\frac{58}{9}-1=\frac{49}{9}$, $x=\frac73\in[2,3)$ - so it is attained.
So no value is removed: (D) is false and the range is $\left(\frac5{37},\frac25\right]$, option (C).

useful_results: On $[k,k+1)$ with $k$ a fixed integer, $[x]=k$: the function reduces to an ordinary function of $x$ and its range is a half-open interval (closed at the left end if the function is decreasing there).
The range of such a piecewise function is the union of the branch ranges; check overlaps of consecutive intervals to see whether gaps arise.
Sup/inf check: a sup is attained only if it occurs at a closed (included) endpoint of its piece.

concepts: Inverse trigonometric equations (identities for tan$^{-1}$ and cos$^{-1}$)
questions.question: Let $S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R:0<x<1\text{ and }2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right)\right\}$. If $n(S)$ denotes the number of elements in $S$ then:
options: $n(S)=2$ and only one element in $S$ is less than $\frac12$
$n(S)=1$ and the element in $S$ is less than $\frac12$
$n(S)=1$ and the element in $S$ is more than $\frac12$
questions.answer: (C) $n(S)=1$ and the element in $S$ is less than $\frac12$
questions.key_idea: Put $x=\tan\theta$ with $\theta\in(0,\frac\pi4)$: the left side becomes $2\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)$ and the right $2\theta$.
solution: Here $\frac\pi4-\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi4\right)$ and $2\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, both inside the principal ranges, so the inverse functions cancel.
So $n(S)=1$ and the element is less than $\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the standard identity $\cos^{-1}\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$ for $x\ge0$, then compare the two $\tan^{-1}$'s directly.

useful_results: $\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)$ for the $\tan(\frac\pi4\mp\theta)$ expansions.
$\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$ and $\tan\frac{3\pi}8=\sqrt2+1$.
Always check that the angle sits inside the principal range before cancelling $\tan^{-1}\tan$ or $\cos^{-1}\cos$.

concepts: Continuity of functions with the greatest integer function
questions.question: If $f(x)=[x]-\left[\frac x4\right]$, $x\in\mathbb R$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer function, then:
options: Both $\lim_{x\to4^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to4^+}f(x)$ exist but are not equal
questions.key_idea: Both $[x]$ and $[x/4]$ jump by $1$ at $x=4$, so the jumps cancel in the difference.
solution: Left limit: for $x<4$ near $4$, $[x]=3$ and $\frac x4<1$ so $\left[\frac x4\right]=0$. $\lim_{x\to4^-}f(x)=3-0=3$.
Right limit: for $x>4$ near $4$, $[x]=4$ and $\frac x4>1$ so $\left[\frac x4\right]=1$. $\lim_{x\to4^+}f(x)=4-1=3$.
LHL $=f(4)=$ RHL, hence $f$ is continuous at $x=4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A greatest-integer term $[kx]$ jumps by $+1$ at each point where $kx$ is an integer; count the jumps of $[x]$ and $[x/4]$ at $x=4$.
solution: $[x]$ jumps by $+1$ at every integer, in particular at $x=4$.
$\left[\frac x4\right]$ jumps by $+1$ at every multiple of $4$, in particular at $x=4$.
The jump of $f=[x]-\left[\frac x4\right]$ at $x=4$ is $1-1=0$, and $f$ is right-continuous, so $f$ is continuous at $4$.
(At $x=3$, only $[x]$ jumps, so $f$ is discontinuous at $3$ - the point $x=4$ is special.)

useful_results: $[x]$ is right-continuous with a jump of $+1$ at each integer; $[kx]$ ($k>0$) jumps at $x=\frac nk$.
For $f=[ax]-[bx]$ jumps can cancel exactly where both terms jump together (at a common point of the two jump sets).
Discontinuities of $[x]-[x/4]$: all integers except multiples of $4$.

concepts: Domain of sum, difference and quotient of functions
questions.question: If the functions are defined as $f(x)=\sqrt x$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{1-x}$, then what is the common domain of the following functions: $f+g$, $f-g$, $f/g$, $g/f$, $g-f$, where $(f\pm g)(x)=f(x)\pm g(x)$, $(f/g)(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$?
questions.key_idea: The sum and difference need $x\in[0,1]$; each quotient additionally needs a non-zero denominator, removing $x=0$ and $x=1$.
solution: For $f+g,\ f-g,\ g-f$ the domain is $D_1\cap D_2=[0,1]$; the quotients need a subset of $[0,1]$.
useful_results: $\text{dom}(f\pm g)=\text{dom}f\cap\text{dom}g$; $\text{dom}\frac fg=\text{dom}f\cap\text{dom}g\cap\{g\ne0\}$.
The common domain of several such combinations is the intersection of all of them: keep every exclusion.
Zeros of the denominator function are excluded even when the numerator also vanishes there (no cancellation in $\frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt{1-x}}$ at $x=1$ - it is just undefined).

concepts: Self-inverse function: $f\circ f=I$
questions.question: For a suitably chosen real constant $a$, let a function $f:\mathbb R-\{-a\}\to\mathbb R$ be defined by $f(x)=\frac{a-x}{a+x}$. Further suppose that for any real number $x\neq-a$ and $f(x)\neq-a$, $(f\circ f)(x)=x$. Then $f\left(-\frac12\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $f(f(x))=x$ for all admissible $x$ forces $(a-1)\left[x^2+(a+1)x-a\right]=0$ identically, so $a=1$.
solution: This must hold for all admissible $x$, and the quadratic $x^2+(a+1)x-a$ cannot vanish for all $x$; hence $a=1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the factor condition as 'a = 1 or x^2 + (a+1)x - a ≠ 0'; the second part is a typo/incorrect statement - the identity must hold for all x, so the quadratic factor cannot vanish identically and a = 1 is forced. The working and the key (A) are otherwise correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: A Mobius map $x\mapsto\frac{px+q}{rx+s}$ is an involution iff its matrix has trace $0$: here trace $=a-1$.
solution: $f\circ f$ corresponds to $M^2=(\operatorname{tr}M)M-(\det M)I$ by Cayley-Hamilton.
$M$ is not scalar (off-diagonal entries $a,1$ are not both $0$), so $M^2$ is scalar (giving the identity map) iff $\operatorname{tr}M=0$.

useful_results: $f(x)=\frac{px+q}{rx+s}$ satisfies $f\circ f=\text{id}$ iff $p+s=0$ (with $ps-qr\ne0$), or $f$ is the identity.
The involution $f(x)=\frac{1-x}{1+x}$ satisfies $f(\tan\theta)=\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)$.
For a function identity such as $f(f(x))=x$, equate coefficients of powers of $x$ after clearing denominators, since it must hold for all $x$.

concepts: Limit of greatest integer functions
questions.question: The set of all values of $a$ for which $\lim_{x\to a}\left([x-5]-[2x+2]\right)=0$, where $[\lambda]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $\lambda$, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Reduce to $[x]-[2x]=7$ near $a$, solve it on the two halves of each unit interval, and drop the end points where the one-sided values differ.
solution: The limit of an integer-valued function exists only if the function is constant near $a$, so we need $[x]-[2x]=7$ for $x$ near $a$ (both sides).
At $a=-7.5$ the left side ($x<-7.5$, $n=-8$ on $[-8,-7.5)$) gives $[x]-[2x]=8\ne7$, so the limit does not exist at $-7.5$.
At $a=-6.5$ the right side ($x\in[-6.5,-6)$) gives $-n-1=6\ne7$, so the limit does not exist at $-6.5$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF finds the interval [-7.5,-7) and then asserts 'limit does not exist at -7.5' with no reason, and its final set (-7.5,-6.5) silently drops -6.5 without any check. Added the two end-point checks (left value 8 at -7.5, right value 6 at -6.5) and the point -7. Key (A) is right.

solution: $\left[x+\frac12\right]$ has a limit at $a$ iff $a+\frac12$ is not an integer, and then the limit is $\left[a+\frac12\right]$.

useful_results: Hermite: $[x]+\left[x+\frac1n\right]+\dots+\left[x+\frac{n-1}n\right]=[nx]$; in particular $[2x]=[x]+\left[x+\frac12\right]$.
$[x+m]=[x]+m$ for integer $m$, so integers inside the bracket can be taken out.
$\lim_{x\to a}[g(x)]$ exists iff $g(a)$ is not an integer approached from the wrong side; check one-sided limits at breakpoints.

concepts: Set theory: inclusion-exclusion (bounds on the intersection)
questions.question: A survey shows that $73\%$ of the persons working in an office like coffee, whereas $65\%$ like tea. If $x$ denotes the percentage of them who like both coffee and tea, then $x$ cannot be:
questions.key_idea: $x=n(C)+n(T)-n(C\cup T)$ with $n(C\cup T)\le100$ gives $x\ge38$, and $x\le\min(73,65)=65$.
solution: Maximum of $n(T\cap C)$ is $65\%$ (when the set $T$ lies completely inside the set $C$).
Among the options, $38,54,63$ lie in $[38,65]$ but $36<38$, so $x$ cannot be $36$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pigeonhole on the complement: only $27\%$ do not like coffee, so at most $27\%$ of the tea lovers can be outside coffee.
solution: $100\%-73\%=27\%$ of the people do not like coffee.
At most $27\%$ of the people can be tea-lovers without liking coffee, so at least $65\%-27\%=38\%$ like both.

useful_results: $\max(0,\,n(A)+n(B)-n(U))\le n(A\cap B)\le\min(n(A),n(B))$.
Similarly $\max(n(A),n(B))\le n(A\cup B)\le\min(n(U),\,n(A)+n(B))$.
For three sets the lower bound is $n(A\cap B\cap C)\ge n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-2n(U)$.

concepts: Even and odd parts of a function
questions.question: Let $f(x)=a^x$ $(a>0)$ be written as $f(x)=f_1(x)+f_2(x)$, where $f_1(x)$ is an even function and $f_2(x)$ is an odd function. Then $f_1(x+y)+f_1(x-y)$ equals:
questions.key_idea: The even part of $a^x$ is $\frac{a^x+a^{-x}}2$; expanding $f_1(x+y)+f_1(x-y)$ factorises into $\left(a^x+a^{-x}\right)\left(a^y+a^{-y}\right)/2$.
solution: Here $f_1(x)=\frac{a^x+a^{-x}}2$ is even and $f_2(x)=\frac{a^x-a^{-x}}2$ is odd.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options with the special value $y=0$, where $f_1(0)=1$ and $f_2(0)=0$.
solution: (A) gives $2f_1(x)f_1(0)=2f_1(x)$ - matches. (B) gives $2f_1(x)^2$, which is not $2f_1(x)$ in general (e.g. $a=2,x=1$: $f_1(1)=1.25$).
(C) and (D) give $2f_1(x)f_2(x)$ and $2f_1(x)f_2(0)=0$ - both wrong. So (A) is the only possible option.

useful_results: Every $f$ splits uniquely as $f=\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}2+\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}2$ (even part plus odd part).
$\frac{a^x+a^{-x}}2=\cosh(x\ln a)$ and $\cosh(u+v)+\cosh(u-v)=2\cosh u\cosh v$ (the hyperbolic analogue of $\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)=2\cos A\cos B$).
Option-elimination with special values ($y=0$ or $x=y$) is fast for identity questions.

concepts: Differentiability and the derivative as a limit
Definite integral of a constant
questions.question: Let $f$ be a differentiable function from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le2|x-y|^{3/2}$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$. If $f(0)=1$ then $\int_0^1f^2(x)\,dx$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $|x-y|$ and letting $x\to y$ gives $f'(y)=0$, since the exponent $\frac32>1$; so $f$ is constant.
solution: Let $x\to y$: the right side tends to $0$, so $|f'(y)|\le0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Without derivatives: chop $[0,x]$ into $n$ equal parts and use the bound on each part; the total variation tends to $0$.
solution: Fix $x>0$ and split $[0,x]$ into $n$ equal parts of length $\frac xn$.

useful_results: A Holder condition $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M|x-y|^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha>1$ forces $f$ to be constant; for $\alpha=1$ it is only Lipschitz (e.g. $f(x)=|x|$).
The same idea: $|f(x)-f(y)|\le(x-y)^2$ for all $x,y$ also implies $f$ constant - a very common exam setup.
The partition argument ($n$ pieces each of size $\frac xn$) shows why the exponent must exceed $1$: the bound $n\left(\frac xn\right)^{\alpha}\to0$ iff $\alpha>1$.

concepts: Relations: reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties
questions.question: Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb R$, given by $R=\{(a,b):3a-3b+\sqrt7\text{ is an irrational number}\}$. Then $R$ is:
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.answer: (B) reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
questions.key_idea: $3(a-a)+\sqrt7=\sqrt7$ is irrational (reflexive); a pair that gives $3(b-a)+\sqrt7=0$ breaks symmetry, and a chain whose composite gives $0$ breaks transitivity.
solution: Reflexive: $3(a-a)+\sqrt7=\sqrt7$, which is irrational, so $(a,a)\in R$; $R$ is reflexive.
Symmetric: take $a=\frac{\sqrt7}3,\ b=0$: $3a-3b+\sqrt7=2\sqrt7$ is irrational, so $(a,b)\in R$.
But $3(b-a)+\sqrt7=-\sqrt7+\sqrt7=0$ is rational, so $(b,a)\notin R$; $R$ is not symmetric.
Transitive: take $(a,b)=\left(\frac{\sqrt7}3,1\right)$: $3\left(\frac{\sqrt7}3-1\right)+\sqrt7=2\sqrt7-3$ is irrational, so $(a,b)\in R$.
But $(a,c)$: $3\left(\frac{\sqrt7}3-\frac{2\sqrt7}3\right)+\sqrt7=0$ is rational, so $(a,c)\notin R$; $R$ is not transitive.
So $R$ is reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive.
useful_results: To disprove a property of a relation, one explicit counterexample is enough; to disprove symmetry, find $(a,b)\in R$ with $(b,a)\notin R$.
For a relation defined through $a-b$, write $d=a-b$: reflexivity tests $d=0$, symmetry tests $d\to-d$, transitivity tests $d_1,d_2\to d_1+d_2$.
A relation defined by '$h(a,b)\notin\mathbb Q$' is likely to fail symmetry/transitivity because the complement ($h\in\mathbb Q$) is the 'nice' set.

concepts: Logarithmic functions and functional identities
questions.question: If $f(x)=\log_e\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)$, $|x|<1$, then $f\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $1\mp\frac{2x}{1+x^2}=\frac{(1\mp x)^2}{1+x^2}$, so the ratio becomes $\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^2$.
useful_results: $\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}$ so $\ln\frac{1-x}{1+x}=-2\tanh^{-1}x$.
$\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ is the tangent-double-angle shape for $\tan$ ($\frac{2t}{1-t^2}$) and the $\tanh$ one for $\tanh$ ($\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$); recognising it gives the identity at once.
Similarly $f\left(\frac{x+y}{1+xy}\right)=f(x)+f(y)$ for $f(x)=\ln\frac{1-x}{1+x}$ (addition formula for $\tanh$).

concepts: Limit involving the greatest integer and modulus functions
questions.question: For each $x\in\mathbb R$, let $[x]$ be the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Then $\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{x([x]+|x|)\sin[x]}{|x|}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: For $x\to0^-$: $[x]=-1$ and $|x|=-x$, so everything reduces to $\sin(-1)$ times a limit of $-(-1+h)$.
useful_results: Near $0^-$: $[x]=-1$; near $0^+$: $[x]=0$. Always write $x=-h$ for left limits and replace $|x|$ by $h$.
$\frac{x}{|x|}=-1$ for $x<0$ and $+1$ for $x>0$ - a common sign factor in such limits.
Because $\sin[x]$ is evaluated at a fixed integer, it is just a constant factor ($\sin(-1)=-\sin1$).

concepts: Inverse trigonometric equations (sum of $\sin^{-1}$ terms)
questions.question: Given that the inverse trigonometric functions take principal values only, the number of real values of $x$ which satisfy $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3x}5\right)+\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{4x}5\right)=\sin^{-1}x$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Take sine of both sides, reduce to $3\sqrt{25-16x^2}+4\sqrt{25-9x^2}=25$ and note the left side is decreasing in $x^2$; then verify each root, since taking $\sin$ may add roots.
solution: So $x=0$ is a root; otherwise divide by $x$ and multiply by $5$: $3\sqrt{\frac{25-16x^2}{25}}+4\sqrt{\frac{25-9x^2}{25}}=5$, i.e. $3\sqrt{25-16x^2}+4\sqrt{25-9x^2}=25$.
At $x^2=1$: $3\cdot3+4\cdot4=25$ holds. The left side strictly decreases as $x^2$ increases, so $x^2=1$ is the only solution, $x=\pm1$.
Cross-check: $x=0$: $0+0=0$. $x=1$: $\sin^{-1}\frac35+\sin^{-1}\frac45=\frac\pi2=\sin^{-1}1$. $x=-1$: both sides change sign, so it also holds.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes '3√(25-16x^2)+4√(25-9x^2)=25, x^2=1' with no argument that x^2=1 is the only root. Added the monotonicity argument and spelled out the checks at 0, 1, -1 (needed because taking sine can introduce extra roots). Key (C) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $A=\sin^{-1}\frac{3x}5,\ B=\sin^{-1}\frac{4x}5$: then $\sin^2A+\sin^2B=x^2$, and $\sin^2(A+B)=x^2$ forces $\sin A\sin B=0$ or $\cos(A+B)=0$.
solution: Use $1-\cos^2B=\sin^2B$ etc.: $2\sin A\sin B\cos A\cos B=2\sin^2A\sin^2B$, i.e. $\sin A\sin B\,(\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B)=0$.
$\cos(A+B)=0$ with $A,B$ of the sign of $x$ gives $A+B=\pm\frac\pi2$, so $\sin^{-1}x=\pm\frac\pi2$ and $x=\pm1$ (check: $\sin^{-1}\frac35+\sin^{-1}\frac45=\frac\pi2$).

useful_results: Equations of the form $\sin^{-1}u+\sin^{-1}v=\sin^{-1}w$: take sine, but verify the roots because $\sin$ is not one-one and $\sin^{-1}$ has the range $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$.
$\sin^{-1}p+\sin^{-1}q=\frac\pi2$ whenever $p^2+q^2=1$ with $p,q\ge0$ (here $\frac35,\frac45$).
$\sin^2A+\sin^2B=\sin^2(A+B)$ iff $\sin A\sin B=0$ or $\cos(A+B)=0$ - useful for sums with a Pythagorean pair.
For $x\in[-1,1]$ domain restrictions come from every inverse trigonometric term; list them first.

concepts: Transitivity of relations
questions.question: Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be two relations defined as follows: $R_1=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a^2+b^2\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $R_2=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a^2+b^2\notin\mathbb Q\}$, where $\mathbb Q$ is the set of all rational numbers. Then:
options: $R_2$ is transitive but $R_1$ is not transitive
$R_1$ is transitive but $R_2$ is not transitive
questions.key_idea: For each relation choose irrational squares like $5\pm\sqrt3$ so that $a^2+b^2$, $b^2+c^2$ are of the required kind but $a^2+c^2$ is not.
solution: But $a^2+c^2=(5+\sqrt3)+(4+\sqrt3)=9+2\sqrt3\notin\mathbb Q$, so $(a,c)\notin R_1$. $R_1$ is not transitive.
But $a^2+c^2=(5+\sqrt3)+(5-\sqrt3)=10\in\mathbb Q$, so $(a,c)\notin R_2$. $R_2$ is not transitive.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 'a^2+c^2 = ... = 9 + 2√36 ∉ Q' for R1 (2√36 = 12 would be rational - the correct value is 9 + 2√3), and labels the second step of R1 and every step of R2 as 'aR1b/aR1c/bR2b' (should be bR1c, and aR2b, bR2c, aR2c with a R2 b: a^2+b^2 = 9+√3). Corrected the value and the labels; key (C) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Both $R_1$ and $R_2$ are symmetric; a symmetric relation that is transitive must be reflexive at every point that is related to something - so find a point where reflexivity fails.
solution: If a symmetric relation is transitive, then $(a,b)\in R$ implies $(b,a)\in R$ and hence $(a,a)\in R$.
$R_1$: take $a=2^{1/4}$ ($a^2=\sqrt2$) and $b=\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}$. Then $a^2+b^2=2\in\mathbb Q$, so $(a,b),(b,a)\in R_1$.
Transitivity would give $(a,a)\in R_1$, but $a^2+a^2=2\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$. So $R_1$ is not transitive.
$R_2$: take $a=1$ and $b=2^{1/4}$. Then $a^2+b^2=1+\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$, so $(a,b),(b,a)\in R_2$.
Transitivity would give $(1,1)\in R_2$, but $1+1=2\in\mathbb Q$. So $R_2$ is not transitive. Hence option (C).

useful_results: A symmetric relation that is transitive and has every element related to something is automatically reflexive ($aRb,bRa\Rightarrow aRa$). So 'symmetric but not reflexive' $\Rightarrow$ not transitive when some element is related to another.
Irrational building blocks: $5\pm\sqrt3$ sum to a rational, $5+\sqrt3$ and $4+\sqrt3$ add to an irrational; use conjugate pairs to control rationality.
For relations on irrational/rational structure, do not forget $\mathbb Q$ is closed under addition: $x\in\mathbb Q,\ y\notin\mathbb Q\Rightarrow x+y\notin\mathbb Q$.

concepts: Inverse trigonometric functions (sum of $\tan^{-1}$)
Logarithmic series expansion
questions.question: If $0<a,b<1$ and $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\frac\pi4$, then the value of $(a+b)-\left(\frac{a^2+b^2}2\right)+\left(\frac{a^3+b^3}3\right)-\left(\frac{a^4+b^4}4\right)+\dots$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\frac\pi4\iff a+b+ab=1$, and the series is $\ln(1+a)+\ln(1+b)=\ln\left[(1+a)(1+b)\right]$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The answer is the same for every admissible pair, so take the symmetric pair $a=b=\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$.
solution: The value does not depend on the pair (by the general solution), so the answer is $\ln2$, option (C).

useful_results: $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\frac\pi4$ (with $0<a,b<1$) $\iff a+b+ab=1\iff(1+a)(1+b)=2$.
$A+B=45^\circ\Rightarrow(1+\tan A)(1+\tan B)=2$ - the classical product identity.
$\ln(1+t)=t-\frac{t^2}2+\frac{t^3}3-\dots$ for $-1<t\le1$; the series $\sum(-1)^{n+1}\frac{a^n+b^n}n$ is then $\ln[(1+a)(1+b)]$.
Questions that say 'then the value of ... is' can be solved with a convenient special case when the result is constant.

concepts: Differentiability of composite functions with modulus
questions.question: Let $f(x)=15-|x-10|$, $x\in\mathbb R$. Then the set of all values of $x$ at which the function $g(x)=f(f(x))$ is not differentiable is:
questions.key_idea: $f(f(x))=15-\left||x-10|-5\right|$ has corners where $|x-10|=0$ and where $|x-10|=5$.
solution: Non-differentiable where $10-x=0$ (inner modulus) and where $|10-x|=5$ (outer modulus).
(Check: near $x=10$, $g=10+|x-10|$, slopes $\mp1$; near $x=5$ and $x=15$ the slope changes sign from $\pm1$ to $\mp1$.)
useful_results: For $h(x)=|u(x)|$ the corners are at the zeros of $u$ where $u'\neq0$, plus corners of $u$ itself (unless cancelled).
For compositions of piecewise-linear 'tent' maps, count kinks as: kinks of the inner map, plus preimages of the kinks of the outer map.
$15-|x-10|$ is a tent with peak $(10,15)$; its second iterate has kinks at $x=10$ and at the two points mapped to $10$ ($x=5,15$).
